analysis.one_liner: Exempts minor league baseball players from federal minimum wage and overtime rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a House vote: it sat in committee for the rest of the 114th Congress and expired when that Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have changed federal wage law so that minor league baseball players — who work long, months-long seasons for their clubs — would no longer be entitled to the federal minimum wage or overtime pay. It also included a retroactive clause saying no club could be sued or punished for past wage violations, which would have erased lawsuits players had already filed. The bill was sent to a House committee, then to a subcommittee, and never came up for a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would have been Major League Baseball club owners, who pay the salaries of affiliated minor league players. They would have been freed from minimum wage and overtime obligations for those players and — through the retroactive immunity clause — shielded from any lawsuits or penalties for wage violations that had already occurred.

how_it_helps.text: It amended the Fair Labor Standards Act to exempt any employee under contract to play minor league baseball from both minimum wage and maximum hours (overtime) requirements.
It also clarified that major league players are not covered by the overtime provision, extending the protection up the ladder.

It barred any liability or punishment for past violations of minimum wage, overtime, or recordkeeping rules — for work performed before the bill's enactment as well as after — which would have ended pending legal claims by players.

analysis.who_pays: Minor league players would have borne the cost: they would lose the federal right to minimum wage and overtime for work that consumes most of their year, and they would lose any ability to recover back pay for violations that had already happened.

drawbacks.text: Exempting minor leaguers from the Fair Labor Standards Act would leave them without any federal guarantee of minimum wage or overtime, even though their seasons run for months and involve near-daily work.
The retroactive immunity in Section 2(b) would have wiped out legal claims already filed by players for unpaid wages, including any case pending at the time of enactment.

Critics of the exemption argued that minor league players are employees in every ordinary sense — they are paid by their clubs, disciplined by them, and cannot freely pursue outside work during the season — so they should not be carved out of wage protections that cover most other workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow almost entirely to MLB team owners: an exemption from wage law going forward and immunity from lawsuits already filed. The costs fall on a few thousand minor league players, who would have had no federal right to minimum wage or overtime during long playing seasons. There is no meaningful public benefit in the bill's text to weigh against that cost; it is a narrow carve-out for one industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House education committee and then to a subcommittee, no one ever brought it to a vote, and it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 24, 2016 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
On September 19, 2016 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, which took no further action on it.
The bill never reached the House floor and expired at the end of the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Minor league players are better off: because the bill died, they kept federal minimum wage and overtime protections and any legal claims for unpaid wages. The clubs did not get the exemption or the retroactive immunity they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Minor league players kept their wage claims

for.name: Rep. Cheri Bustos
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor, making the introduction bipartisan.

for.name: Major League Baseball and its affiliated minor league clubs
for.what_they_did: The bill tracked the industry's position that minor league players should be exempt from wage law, and press reporting at the time identified baseball's clubs as the proposal's driving backers.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Workforce Protections and never scheduled a markup or floor action, letting it expire.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Republican with a Democratic original cosponsor, but it drew only one additional cosponsor and no recorded floor opposition, since it never advanced out of committee.

industries.industry: Major League Baseball club owners (who fund and control affiliated minor league teams)
industries.note: The bill would have shielded the clubs that pay minor league players from federal minimum wage and overtime rules, and would have retroactively erased liability for unpaid wages already claimed in court. For owners, the bill's whole value is paying less and owing nothing back.

Players are the group the bill takes from, not gives to: they would lose federal wage protections and any claims for back pay. Since players are workers rather than an industry, this entry captures the other side of the owners' gain.
